newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Malan sees growth, rules out devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Malan sees growth, rules out devaluation.

text.p: The Brazilian economy will grow by between four and five percent in 1997 and inflation will be below ten percent, Finance Minister Pedro Malan said.
The federal government should show a primary surplus of 1.5 percent in 1997, rising to 2.0 percent in subsequent years, Malan told reporters.
He also ruled out the need to devalue the Brazilian real currency in response to the country's swelling trade deficit.
"We are not going to have a maxi-devaluation of the real in response to the pressure and nervousness shown by some regarding the country's external situaion," Malan said.

Even if predictions of an $8.0 billion trade deficit next year proved correct, that figure would represent only one percent of Brazil's gross domestic product which is expected to gross $800 billion next year, he said.
Brazil's trade deficit in 1996 is expected to be about $4.5 billion.

The effect of measures to boost exports taken earlier this year would begin to be felt in 1997 and rising foreign direct investment in 1997, higher than the $8.0 billion seen in 1996, would also ease trade deficit concerns, Malan said.
The minister repeated his view that receipts from Brazil's privatization program should be used to reduce the country's debt stockpile.

Earlier this week, Communications Minister Sergio Motta said he believed revenues from the upcoming privatization of Brazil's telecommunications industry should be pumped into improving the country's ailing infrastructure.
Malan recognized differences existed within the government on the issue and said the last word would be with President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
